toc.title: Tool Design for the Agent-Computer Interface

html:
1What You Will Learn

Note

Acronyms in this note. MCP: Model Context Protocol; CRM: customer relationship management; BM25: Best Matching 25, a keyword ranking function

  • What capability bloat is and how it harms cost, accuracy and security
  • How to audit a tool and agent configuration
  • Progressive discovery: tool search, deferred loading, code execution with MCP
  • Monolithic context versus progressive discovery: when each wins
  • Tool design for the agent-computer interface

2Capability Bloat

Running case

Lumen Advisory Audits a Support Agent With 140 Tools

  • A client connected five MCP servers to one agent: ticketing, billing, CRM, wiki and monitoring
  • The agent now carries 140 tool definitions, picks the wrong tool, answers slowly and costs more
  • It can also change billing plans and close accounts, though support staff only read tickets and draft replies

Capability bloat = more tools, permissions and context than the role needs.

Harm Evidence
Tokens and latency A multi-server setup (for example five common servers) can use about 55k tokens of definitions before any work
Accuracy Tool selection degrades beyond about 30 to 50 tools
Security Every tool is attack surface: a successful injection can use any tool the agent holds
Cost and caching Larger prefixes cost more and can be disturbed by changes
Maintenance More descriptions to keep consistent

Audit questions

  1. Which tools does this role actually need? Remove the rest (least privilege).
  2. Are descriptions distinct enough that two tools are not confused?
  3. Can several fine-grained tools be merged into one well-designed tool?
  4. Which tools are used rarely: candidates for deferred loading?
  5. Does any tool allow destructive or irreversible actions without a gate?
Exam tip

The first fix for excess capability is to remove tools the role does not need (least privilege). Logging or confirmation prompts are compensating controls, not removal of the privilege.

3Progressive Discovery

Instead of loading everything, expose capabilities on demand.

Mechanism How it works Notes
Tool search tool Mark tools defer_loading: true; the model searches the catalog (regex or BM25 variant) and only matches load All definitions are still sent in tools; at least one tool stays non-deferred; keep the 3 to 5 most used tools non-deferred; up to 10,000 tools; typically cuts definition tokens by over 85%
Custom search Your own tool (embeddings) returns tool_reference blocks For semantic matching
MCP toolsets Set defer_loading in the mcp_toolset default or per tool Aggregating many servers
Code execution with MCP Present servers as a code API in a file tree; the agent lists and reads only needed files, and filters data in code Example reduction from about 150,000 to 2,000 tokens; needs a secure sandbox
Skills Metadata always, instructions on trigger For procedures
  • Use tool search when you have 10 or more tools, definitions over 10k tokens, tool accuracy dropping, or many MCP servers (hundreds of tools). Standard calling is fine under about 10 tools or when every tool is used on every request.
  • Naming: use consistent prefixes (github_, slack_) and keywords in descriptions so one search finds a whole group; add a system-prompt line describing the categories.
  • Caching: a deferred tool cannot carry cache_control; deferred loading keeps the cached prefix stable.
  • Code execution keeps intermediate data out of the model (a 10,000-row sheet filtered to a few rows) and can tokenize sensitive values; its cost is the sandbox's operational and security overhead.

Monolithic versus progressive

Monolithic context Progressive discovery
Fits Small, stable tool or knowledge sets; every item used each time Large or growing catalogs; rare use
Pros Simple; cache-friendly; no search step Fewer tokens; better selection; scales
Cons Bloat, confusion, cost at scale Extra search step and latency; needs good names and descriptions

4Tool Design for the Agent-Computer Interface

  • Treat tool design like interface design: invest as much as in a human UI.
  • Write descriptions like a docstring for a junior developer: purpose, parameters, examples, edge cases, boundaries from similar tools.
  • Poka-yoke: make mistakes hard (for example, require absolute paths).
  • Choose formats the model writes easily; avoid overhead such as counting lines.
  • Return only what the next step needs; keep tool results compact and structured, with clear error messages.
  • Test with many inputs, observe mistakes, iterate; one team spent more time on tools than on the prompt.
Exam tip

Deferred tools are still sent in tools; deferral only keeps them out of the context until found.

Exam tip

Use tool search from about 10 tools or 10k tokens of definitions; under that, plain tool calling is simpler.

5Exam Q&A

S1A procurement agent can read purchase orders, draft supplier emails, approve payments and cancel contracts, but buyers only need it to read orders and draft emails. Which change best reduces risk?

  • ASwap in a larger model that follows the instruction "never pay without approval" more closely
  • BKeep every tool and show a confirmation dialog before payments and cancellations
  • CRemove the payment-approval and contract-cancellation tools from this agent's configuration
  • DKeep every tool and write each approval and cancellation to an audit log for later review
Show the answer

Answer: C. Least privilege removes the unneeded capability; logs and dialogs only compensate for it.

S2An agent connected to five MCP servers carries 140 tools and often calls the wrong one. What should the architect try?

  • AAdd a paragraph to the system prompt listing all 140 tools
  • BIncrease max_tokens so that the model can think longer about the choice among the hundred and forty tools
  • CDefer most tools with the tool search tool, keeping a few frequently used tools loaded
  • DSplit the tool list in half and load a random half per request to reduce the overall token count
Show the answer

Answer: C. Deferred loading with search reduces definition tokens and selection confusion.

S3For which situation is standard tool calling (without tool search) the better fit?

  • AA library of several hundred tools that grows monthly as each team adds its own integrations
  • BAn aggregation of many MCP servers
  • CTool definitions that total more than 10k tokens
  • DSix small tools that are all used on nearly every request
Show the answer

Answer: D. Few, always-used, small tools do not need discovery.

S4An agent processes a 10,000-row spreadsheet through tool calls and runs out of context. Which approach addresses the cause?

  • ALet the agent filter the data in code inside a sandbox and return only the few relevant rows
  • BAsk the model to remember all rows in its own words
  • CRaise the effort level so that the model reads faster
  • DPaste the full sheet into the system prompt to avoid tool calls, accepting the larger context cost
Show the answer

Answer: A. Keeping intermediate results out of the model saves tokens and errors.

S5Which TWO are valid statements about the tool search tool? Select TWO.

  • AIt can only be used with a single tool
  • BAll tool definitions are still sent in the request; deferred ones load into context only when found
  • CDeferred tools can carry cache_control breakpoints
  • DDeferring a tool also removes it from the request payload
  • EAt least one tool must remain non-deferred, and the search tool itself is never deferred
Show the answer

Answer: B, E. Deferral controls what enters the context, not what is sent.

S6What is the main trade-off of progressive discovery compared with a monolithic context?

  • ANo difference in latency or accuracy
  • BBetter caching but no ability to scale to many tools
  • CFewer tokens and better selection at scale, at the cost of an extra search step and the need for good descriptions
  • DHigher token use but no need for descriptions
Show the answer

Answer: C. Discovery trades a search step for lean context.

S7Which tool-design practice reduces misuse by the model?

  • AOverlapping tools so the model can pick any of several
  • BShort names and one-word descriptions to save tokens
  • CDescriptions with examples, edge cases and clear boundaries from similar tools, plus arguments that are hard to misuse
  • DHiding error messages to avoid confusing the model
Show the answer

Answer: C. Clear interfaces and poka-yoke design lower error rates.

6Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Bloat About 55k tokens for five servers; accuracy falls beyond 30 to 50 tools; more attack surface
First fix Remove tools the role does not need
Tool search Defer; regex or BM25; keep 3 to 5 loaded; use at 10+ tools or over 10k tokens
Code execution with MCP Code API in a file tree; filter in sandbox; about 98.7% token saving in the example
Monolithic Simple, cache-friendly, small stable sets
ACI Docstring-quality descriptions, examples, poka-yoke, compact results
